units.translation: ⟦1⟧ (⟦2⟧) he is the interpreter of the signs, and the appearance of these women is, and they themselves are, a ⟦3⟧ (cf. ⟦4⟧ ⟦5⟧ the dragon of the dream; ⟦6⟧). After the Pythia has departed, the doors of the temple open for the spectator, and the interior becomes visible to him, just as the Pythia described it; yet beside Orestes now stands also Apollo, and beside him Hermes. The machinery employed was surely the same as ⟦7⟧ (⟦8⟧), although the scholiast on the Choephori speaks of the ekkyklema, here of ⟦9⟧ (cf. Introduction p. 15), and certainly here too the picture displayed was an extremely effective one. G. Hermann, to be sure, placed the ekkyklema before v. 94, so that the Erinyes, as they became visible, would not draw all the attention of the audience to themselves; as long, however, as they sleep and rest, this is by no means the case. I also do not think (cf. below) that Orestes still sits in the background, but rather that Apollo has already led him past the Erinyes into the foreground, whereby these were to some extent concealed (cf. v. Wilamowitz, Translation p. 52). Then Orestes no longer needs to walk past them. According to Kirchhoff, the words of Orestes to Apollo, 85-87, must stand here first. As transmitted, one must presuppose that such a request of Orestes has already taken place; for otherwise Apollo could not begin as he does. Worse is that Orestes' words now sound as if the god had not yet promised any care at all, and again, in what he says further, he in no way refers to the request with a new promise, but rather the first verse: ⟦10⟧ emphasizes what he himself said last. So what Orestes says is now nothing but a useless and ineffective interruption. But if one transposes, the person of Orestes, already indicated to the spectators, properly introduces the person of Apollo, not yet indicated as present: ⟦11⟧, and one must presuppose that Apollo has made him stand up and led him to the entrance, so that he may now continue his journey, after the purpose of his coming, the purification, has been fulfilled. Naturally Orestes is afraid: he acknowledges that Apollo has performed what he promised and has purified him, but his further care is still necessary. Thus the device of transposition, as already at v. 20 and in the Choephori several times, is again required here, and the cause of the disorder must be, as ⟦12⟧, the wandering of the eye from one paragraphos to another. The scholiast (see on 64) seems already to have had the wrong order. In Athens, in accounts, one distinguished between ⟦13⟧ and ⟦14⟧ (Hesychius); Orestes feels secure with the god with regard to the former, also according to what he himself has experienced; but the god must first prove his care. The words contain no reproach; but they also do not sound, as Weil says, modest. "Since the one thing is so easy for you, you can do something extra and learn the other as well." Orestes is ⟦15⟧ of the god; this gives him, in relation to the latter, a certain dignity, see v. 233 f. ⟦16⟧ and ⟦17⟧ with the vowel combination frequent in ⟦18⟧ (⟦19⟧ attributed in f h; in M corr. there is aphaeresis of the ⟦20⟧-; according to Dindorf crasis to ⟦21⟧-), see Kühner-Blass I, 242. ⟦22⟧ (also 581) beside ⟦23⟧ ⟦24⟧, 982, see ibid. II, 68, 4 (also Pindar both, Pyth. 3, 80, 8, 7). ⟦25⟧ ⟦26⟧ (with inf.) and often in the same play.
